cards.front: What does the polarization of a wave describe?
cards.back: The path traced by the tip of $\mathbf{E}$ over time at a fixed point in space, seen with the wave travelling away from or toward you.

cards.front: General phasor for a wave toward $+z$ with both transverse components?
cards.back: $$\tilde{\mathbf{E}}=(\hat{\mathbf{x}}a_x+\hat{\mathbf{y}}a_ye^{j\delta})e^{-jkz}$$$a_x,a_y\ge0$; $\delta$ is the phase of the $y$ component relative to $x$.

cards.front: When is a wave linearly polarized?
cards.back: When $\delta=0$ or $\delta=\pm180^\circ$, or when one component is zero. $\mathbf{E}$ then swings back and forth along a fixed line.

cards.front: Angle of a linearly polarized field from the $x$ axis?
When is a wave circularly polarized?
cards.back: When $a_x=a_y$ and $\delta=\pm90^\circ$. The magnitude of $\mathbf{E}$ stays constant while its direction turns once per period.

cards.front: Left- or right-handed: how to tell (wave toward $+z$)?
cards.back: $0<\delta<180^\circ$: left-handed. $-180^\circ<\delta<0$: right-handed. Point the thumb along the direction of travel; the fingers of that hand curl the way $\mathbf{E}$ turns.

Phasor forms of LHC and RHC waves toward $+z$?
What do you get by adding equal LHC and RHC waves?
cards.back: A linearly polarized wave. The rotating parts cancel along one axis and add along the other.

cards.front: Does the handedness change if the wave travels toward $-z$?
cards.back: The time behaviour at a point is the same, but the direction of travel is reversed, so the same $\delta$ gives the opposite handedness. Always check against the direction of travel.

cards.front: Why does polarization matter for antennas?
cards.back: A receiving antenna only picks up the component of the wave that matches its own polarization. A vertical dipole receives nothing from a horizontally polarized wave, and half the power from a circular one.
